preamble: Araucaria says: Solutions whose clues are not given in the numbered list form an alphabet all of whose members are of a kind; their clues are usually partial. These solutions are to be fitted into the remaining spaces jigsaw-wise, wherever they will go.

clue.text: Small boy or girl failed exam at beginning of term

indicators.note: whoever failed has dropped out of the running, so that part is struck from the longer word

parts.note: a viva voce is an oral examination
Viv is a short form of both Vivian and Vivien, so it fits a boy or a girl

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: first letter of term

explanation.surface: A young pupil flunks an exam right at the start of the school term.
explanation.walkthrough: Take VIV out of VIVA VOCE to leave AVOCE, then add T. As with every alphabet entry, the bird itself is defined only by the preamble: this is the A of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The avocet is a black-and-white wading bird with an upturned bill, supplying the letter A in the puzzle's alphabet of birds.

clue.text: Meat covered with iron and served with fire

indicators.note: a covering goes all round what it covers, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a kind of meat

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction: meat cooked on an iron grill and brought to the table in flames.
explanation.walkthrough: The iron symbol FE is split around LAMB.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish described as flambé has had spirits poured over it and set alight just before it is brought to the table.

indicators.note: the word declares itself twisted, so its first couple of letters are turned about

parts.note: the opening letters of the word itself, which it tells you to twist
thatch is jokey slang for a thick head of hair

explanation.walkthrough: A partial clue with no definition: the preamble supplies 'bird', the N of the alphabet. 'Untwisted' is read as UN twisted, giving NU, then THATCH.
explanation.definitionFit: The nuthatch is a small woodland bird that climbs head-first down tree trunks, providing the N entry in this bird alphabet.

clue.text: Partner to ruff holding two of trumps — I have to recover

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so the outer word grips the rest

parts.note: a reeve is the female of the ruff, a wading bird

indicators.note: two of a word means just a couple of its letters, taken from the front

parts.note: the first two letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bridge player holding a couple of trumps hopes to get back into the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruff' looks like trumping at cards, but it is the bird whose female is the reeve. 'two of trumps' means its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrieve something is to get it back again, which is what recovering a lost item means.

clue.text: Not sure could be better — to hit nail on head?

parts.note: the hesitating noise of someone unsure

indicators.note: what a word could be is another possible version of it, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone unsure whether things could be better, wondering if they have hit the nail on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: The umbrette is also called the hammerkop or hammerhead, for its hammer-shaped head; the question mark flags that cryptic definition. It is the U of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Its other name, hammerhead, describes a crest and bill shaped like a hammer, the tool you would hit a nail with.

parts.note: wood (or wode) is an old word for mad or furious
pecker means spirit or courage, as in 'keep your pecker up'

explanation.walkthrough: A partial clue: the preamble supplies the bird, the W of the alphabet. 'Keep your pecker up' is a British phrase meaning keep cheerful; wood for mad survives in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodpecker is the tree-drilling bird that fills the W slot in this alphabet of birds.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the armed services, the one at sea
second meaning: a dark blue colour

explanation.surface: A church service or a waiter's service taken under the shade of a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shade' suggests shadow, but it is a shade of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the seagoing armed service and the dark blue colour of its uniforms.

indicators.note: turning the phrase over swaps the order of its two words before you read across the join

parts.note: the tail of the name, which comes first once the words swap
the head of the rank, which follows straight on

explanation.surface: A historical note on something included by the famous French general.
explanation.walkthrough: Marshal Saxe was an 18th-century French general. Swap his rank and name to 'Saxe Marshal' and the letters spanning the join, saXE MArshal, are the included word. The X of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Xema is the genus name of Sabine's gull, one of very few bird names beginning with X, hence its place here.

clue.text: Introduction to concession with time for consideration

parts.note: though is the word that introduces a concession, as in 'though it rained'
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Opening a concession while allowing time for consideration, like a negotiator stalling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Introduction to' usually means a first letter, but here it is the whole word that introduces a concessive clause.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving something thought means giving it careful consideration; the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Look up the second apocalyptic horse

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: in Revelation the second horseman rides a red horse; a nag is a horse

explanation.surface: Looking up in Revelation which of the four horses comes second.
explanation.walkthrough: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse ride white, red, black and pale horses. The G of the bird alphabet is the male goose.
explanation.definitionFit: A gander is British slang for a quick look, as in 'have a gander'; it is also a male goose.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the enchanter of Arthurian legend
second meaning: a small falcon, F being the alphabet's falcon entry

explanation.surface: An enchanting letter F.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-word partial clue: 'F' points to the F of the bird alphabet, the falcon, of which this is a small species. It is the M of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to King Arthur's wizard, the great enchanter, and to a small fast falcon of moors and coasts.

indicators.note: coming after something means being placed behind it in the line

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five
ult. (ultimo) means of last month, so a letter written in August calls July's dates 'ult.'
a flower is something that flows, a river; the Ure is a Yorkshire river

explanation.surface: A flower that blooms after the fifth of July.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' wants to be a bloom; it is a river. 'the fifth of July' is read as '5th ult.', old business-letter style. The V of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The vulture is a large carrion-eating bird of prey, filling the V position in this alphabet of birds.

clue.text: How bulls express anger at charge for barge?

parts.note: cattle low, making the sound moo
rage is fury or anger

explanation.surface: Angry bulls protesting at what they are being charged to tie up a barge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' sounds like a bull charging but means a fee.
explanation.definitionFit: Moorage is the fee paid for the right to tie a boat up at a mooring, so it is what a barge is charged.

parts.note: the pronoun for a man, with the possessive linking it to what follows
ave is the Latin word of greeting, hail

explanation.surface: The way a Pullman attendant welcomes passengers aboard the luxury train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pullman's' must be split into Pull + man's; a Pullman is a luxury railway carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: To heave is to haul or drag with great effort, which is a strong kind of pulling.

clue.text: Mothball vehicle in which speedo doesn't register?

indicators.note: something in which other things sit is their container, so it wraps them

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
a speedometer showing nothing reads miles per hour zero, MPH 0

explanation.surface: A car laid up in storage, so its speedometer never moves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mothball' looks like a verb about laying up the car, but it is the noun defined; the zero reading is the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Camphor is the strong-smelling substance traditionally used to make mothballs that keep moths off stored clothes.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a mild British swear word adding emphasis
second meaning: reddish in colour, as a healthy complexion

explanation.surface: Something that deepens the colour red.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, but 'Intensifier' and 'of red' are separate meanings; ruddy as a softened 'bloody' is British.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective serves as a polite British emphatic replacing a stronger oath, and also describes a reddish, rosy colour.

clue.text: A series was first backed by a Sussex town

parts.note: taken as written
a run is a series, as a run of wins

indicators.note: something backed goes into reverse, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: whoever was first led

explanation.surface: A sporting run led from the front, with support from a town in Sussex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed by' sounds like sponsorship, but 'backed' reverses and 'by a' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Arundel is a small historic town in West Sussex, England, famous for its castle, seat of the Dukes of Norfolk.

clue.text: Physio etc directed towards setter in river

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it

parts.note: the Trent is a major English river
aimed at
the setter refers to themself as me

explanation.surface: A physiotherapy session pointed at the setter while they stand in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' is the crossword compiler, ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Physiotherapy and similar therapies are kinds of medical treatment, so 'etc' widens the example to the general noun.

indicators.note: to lose the head is to drop the top, here the opening letter

parts.note: to regret is to express sorrow, as in 'we regret any inconvenience'

explanation.surface: Saying sorry for having lost one's head in anger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' suggests losing one's temper, but it removes the first letter. The E of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The egret is a white heron with fine breeding plumes, filling the E place in this alphabet of birds.

clue.text: Read me to promote peace for South American diplomacy

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, the South American city
tact is diplomatic sensitivity

explanation.surface: Reading out a peace proposal as part of South American diplomacy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the answer itself: the Riot Act was a British law read aloud to order crowds to disperse.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the 1714 statute, magistrates read a proclamation to a mob, ordering it to break up and restore order and quiet.

parts.note: tan is crushed tree bark used in tanning leather
a door is an entrance

explanation.surface: A dog barking at the oven door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' looks like a dog's noise; it is tree bark.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandoor is a cylindrical clay oven used in Indian and Central Asian cooking, heated by charcoal.

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so a letter drops out

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin
the letter lost is I, one; the printed 'by 100' does not obviously yield it and may be a garbled 'one'

explanation.surface: A racehorse beaten by a hundred lengths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' looks like a racehorse but is drug slang. Removing I, the Roman one, leaves the bird; how 'by 100' signals that letter is unclear from the clue as printed. The H of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The heron is a tall grey wading bird that stalks fish in shallow water, filling the H slot of the alphabet.

clue.text: He said what another said about the Pope

definitions.text: He said what another said about the Pope

parts.note: surface reading: someone repeating another person's words about the Pope
setter's reading: the archaic 'said he' form that a reporter of speech uses, fitting the papal theme of the puzzle

explanation.surface: Someone passing on gossip they heard about the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic phrase is how an old narrator reports another's speech; the clue describes the phrase rather than giving wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The old-fashioned formula, with the verb before the pronoun, simply means 'he said', reporting someone else's words.

parts.note: surface reading: something moving around the region, like the bird flying about
setter's reading: money circulates, and this is Guatemala's currency

explanation.surface: Something going around Central America.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird gives its name to Guatemala's currency unit, which is what 'circulates'. The Q of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Guatemala's monetary unit is named after its national bird, a brilliant green trogon, and coins and notes are what circulate.

parts.note: OC is Officer Commanding
the future is what is to be
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A commander-in-waiting who has timed things perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Future commander' reads as a cadet, but splits as commander OC followed by 'to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: October is a month, and a month is a period of time in the calendar, so a specific example.

indicators.note: something done over has been beaten up and knocked about out of shape

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spitz dog has had a great lump of a man beaten up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'done' does double duty: it is fodder, and 'done over' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian elkhound is a breed within the spitz group of dogs, with a curled tail and pointed ears.

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one, first
bis is Latin for twice, used to call for a repeat

explanation.walkthrough: A partial clue: the preamble supplies the bird, the I of the alphabet. Bis is used in music and street numbering to mark something repeated.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a wading bird with a long down-curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt, and fills the I slot.

clue.text: County town with duke left for dead on Great North Road

definitions.note: the definition names a place by where it is, rather than as a noun

indicators.note: one thing for another means it stands in that other's place

parts.note: Bedford is the county town of Bedfordshire, and there is a Duke of Bedford
L is the abbreviation for left
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: A county town whose duke has been left for dead beside the old main road north.
explanation.walkthrough: The Great North Road, now the A1, runs from London to Edinburgh; Belford is a small Northumberland town on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Belford lies on the A1 in Northumberland, the historic Great North Road linking London and Edinburgh.

parts.note: Cornwall is in the far south-west of England, SW
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: A property advert: Cornwall available to rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to let' suggests a rental notice; 'let' means allow. The S of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The swallow is a fork-tailed summer migrant bird, supplying the S entry in the puzzle's bird alphabet.

clue.text: Developments for three (not counting the press)

definitions.meaning: first meaning: housing developments
second meaning: the three traditional orders of the realm, the press being the fourth

explanation.surface: Building projects meant for three people, leaving out the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The three estates of the realm are clergy, nobility and commons; the press is called the Fourth Estate.
explanation.definitionFit: Housing estates are planned developments, and the old social orders are called the three estates of the realm.

clue.text: Not so much as a dinner plate

parts.words: Not so much as a dinner
parts.note: tea is a lighter meal than dinner
an L-plate is the sign a British learner driver displays

explanation.surface: Something smaller than a dinner plate, like a side plate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dinner plate' reads as one item, but splits after 'dinner'. An L-plate is the red L sign on a British learner's car. The T of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small dabbling duck with a green wing patch, providing the T in the alphabet.

indicators.note: something formed has been shaped into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: A fish forming the foundation of a fool, the creamy fruit dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: A fool is also a British fruit-and-cream pudding, which makes the surface a recipe.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea bass is a marine food fish, so it is a specific kind of the general term in the clue.

clue.text: Cause of disease (mosquito, largely) to bones would come naturally to the Pope

definitions.text: would come naturally to the Pope
definitions.note: a phrase describing a trait, standing for the noun

indicators.note: largely means only in large part, so the word is cut short

parts.note: a germ causes disease
Anopheles is the malaria-carrying mosquito
the ilia are the hip bones, plural of ilium

explanation.surface: Medical notes on malaria and bones, oddly followed by a remark about the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the start of the mosquito's name is kept. The Pope at the time, Benedict XVI, was German.
explanation.definitionFit: Love of Germany and things German would be natural for a German-born pontiff such as Benedict XVI.

indicators.note: a vagrant wanders about with no fixed place, so the letters roam

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A wandering relative somewhere within reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vagrant' looks like a noun for a tramp but works as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is a family member, so this informal word is an example of a relative.

clue.text: Horse — a very thin one — favourite becomes outsider

parts.note: the zebra is a striped wild horse

indicators.note: to become the outsider is to move to the outside and wrap round

parts.note: a pet is a favourite
a rake is a very thin person

explanation.surface: Racing talk: a scrawny horse, once the favourite, now an outsider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'favourite' and 'outsider' sound like betting terms. The zebra parakeet is another name for the budgerigar. The Z of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The zebra parakeet, the budgerigar, is named for its barred plumage and fills the hard Z slot of the alphabet.

clue.text: Visit in Rhodesia, part 2: a saxifrage

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it

parts.note: split the word as Rhod and esia, taking the second part
to call on someone is to visit

explanation.surface: A travel log: the second part of a visit to Rhodesia, with a note on a saxifrage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part 2' reads like an episode heading, but means the latter part of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Escallonia is a flowering shrub once classified in the saxifrage family, so the setter treats it as one of them.

parts.note: red is the colour of the political left
a poll is a vote, here one won

explanation.surface: A left-wing party winning an election.
explanation.walkthrough: A left-wing win would be a red poll. The R of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The redpoll is a small finch with a red patch on its forehead, giving the R entry in this bird alphabet.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb
second meaning: a prank or spree

explanation.surface: A prank pulled at a sports event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' is read as frolicking, matching the verb sense. The L of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: To lark about means to play or frolic, and a lark is also a bit of mischievous fun, a caper.

parts.note: surface reading: an adhesive label
setter's reading: a shellfish that clings to a ship's hull

explanation.walkthrough: The bottom is a ship's underside, where the crustacean clings. The barnacle goose gives the B of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: This crustacean fixes itself permanently to rocks and ships' hulls, and the barnacle goose shares its name.

clue.text: Branch arrangement simpler without a friend coming in

indicators.note: something coming in enters the middle of another word
without means lacking, so a letter goes

parts.note: simpler means easier
taken as written, the letter removed
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Arranging branches is simpler without a friend butting in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' does real work: it is the letter dropped from the synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An espalier is a fruit tree trained flat against a wall, its limbs tied in a regular framework.

parts.note: a jack is a young pike, a fish

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came

parts.note: a wad is old British army slang for a sandwich or bun

explanation.surface: A fish sandwich sent back by the person collecting the orders.
explanation.walkthrough: Wad is old NAAFI slang for a bun or sandwich. The J of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Jackdaws are famous for picking up and hoarding bright objects, which makes the bird a thieving collector.

clue.text: Scottish island's just like that at an early age

parts.note: Jura is an island in the Inner Hebrides, plus the possessive S
sic means thus, written just like that

explanation.surface: Someone who lived on a Scottish island as a child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at an early age' reads as childhood, but means from a geological age long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jurassic is a geological period around 200 to 145 million years ago, an early age of the Earth.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a counting number such as one, two, three
second meaning: a senior churchman, who wears a red hat

explanation.surface: A number wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Also the red songbird of North America, the C of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Counting numbers are cardinal numbers, and a prince of the Church is marked by the red hat he receives.

parts.note: to term something is to call it that
taken as written
E is slang for the drug Ecstasy

explanation.surface: A hillside resident describes their life up there as pure ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hill dweller' suggests a person; the hill is a termite mound.
explanation.definitionFit: Termites build large earth mounds, and they live inside them, so the insect lives in a hill.

clue.text: Characteristic of the alphabet reported from Brideshead

indicators.note: a report is something said, so we go by sound rather than spelling

parts.note: the puzzle's alphabet is made of birds, and birds are known for this

explanation.surface: A feature of the alphabet described in Brideshead Revisited.
explanation.walkthrough: Flyte is the aristocratic family name in Evelyn Waugh's novel Brideshead Revisited, including Sebastian Flyte.
explanation.definitionFit: Sebastian and Julia Flyte belong to the family whose house is Brideshead in Waugh's novel.

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it

parts.note: façon is French for manner or style
L for learner, a student

explanation.surface: A student dressed in the French fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The cedilla is dropped in crossword grids. The F of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The falcon is a fast bird of prey with long pointed wings, providing the F slot of this alphabet.

definitions.note: W is the alphabet's woodpecker, so the answer is one of those

indicators.note: a return trip goes back the way it came

parts.note: an elf and a fay are both fairy spirits

explanation.surface: The letter W bringing back the spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: W is 6-down in the alphabet, the woodpecker; the yaffle is the green woodpecker, named for its laughing call. It is the Y of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Yaffle is a country name for the green woodpecker, so it is a kind of the bird filling the W entry.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a brief period
second meaning: a magic charm that holds someone bound

explanation.surface: A short-term contract may still be legally binding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'binding' reads as obligatory; it describes a charm that binds.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a brief stretch of time and an enchantment that holds its victim captive.

parts.note: to part is to leave
a ridge is a long stretch of high ground

explanation.surface: An order to come down from the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: A partial clue made purely of wordplay; the preamble supplies the bird, the P of the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The partridge is a plump brown game bird of farmland, supplying the P entry in the alphabet.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one who baptises by plunging people under water

definitions.note: only the Big form of the name is the Great Bear
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the American name for the Plough, the bright stars of the Great Bear

explanation.surface: John the Baptist's large bear.
explanation.walkthrough: The Big Dipper is the American name for the Plough, part of Ursa Major. The D of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anabaptist was nicknamed a dipper for full immersion, and the Big Dipper is the star pattern within Ursa Major.

clue.text: Bored with tennis centre, turn into spectator

indicators.note: to go into something is to be placed inside it

parts.note: an eye is something that watches
a U-turn, U

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letters

parts.note: the two middle letters of the six

explanation.surface: A tennis spectator bored with the centre court, ready to turn away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tennis centre' suggests a venue; it means the middle letters of 'tennis'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennuyé is French borrowed into English for someone weary and listless, suffering from ennui.

clue.text: I can give new floor to newspaper in capital (new)

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed by it

parts.note: Lima is the capital of Peru
the FT is the Financial Times
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A flooring firm advertising new floors to a newspaper in the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new floor' suggests flooring, but the definition speaks as the answer: he takes you to a different floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A lift attendant operates the elevator, taking passengers up or down to another storey of the building.

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: not given the OK
second meaning: a small alcove or corner

explanation.walkthrough: The answer splits as NO OK, which is what unauthorised means; 'recess' looks like a parliamentary break but is an alcove.
explanation.definitionFit: A nook is a small sheltered corner or alcove, which is the same thing as a recess in a wall.

clue.text: Bit of a hill for Charles and Cromwell?

parts.note: Charles was a king, K
Old Noll was a nickname for Oliver Cromwell

explanation.surface: A hill fought over in the English Civil War between Charles I and Cromwell.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles I and Cromwell were the opposing leaders of the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: A knoll is a small rounded hillock, so it is a modest piece of a hill or a little hill.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: old RAF slang for an aeroplane, like crate
second meaning: a box-shaped flying toy on a string, so a box may be one

explanation.surface: A crate may serve as a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crate' looks like a packing case, but is slang for an old aircraft. The K of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both kite and crate were airmen's slang for an aircraft, and a box kite is a common kind of flying kite.

clue.text: Partners keeping large beast in cattle shed?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside

parts.note: South and North are partners at bridge
a hippopotamus is a large beast

explanation.surface: Farmers keeping an enormous animal in the cow shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Bridge partners sit North-South and East-West.
explanation.definitionFit: Shippon is a dialect word, mainly northern English, for a cowshed or byre where cattle are housed.

indicators.note: without means outside, so one piece surrounds the other
something disclosed has been laid open and its parts rearranged

parts.note: the number written as a word
the in French is le

explanation.surface: A second item revealed but missing its translation.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' looks like a cross-reference to 2-down but is just the number; 'without' means outside, not lacking. The O of the bird alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: An owlet is a young owl, which fills the O entry in this alphabet of birds.

parts.note: going out
a train is a line, as a train of thought or a line of vehicles

explanation.surface: A drawing of a train pulling out of the station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'train' suggests a railway; it means a line or sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: An outline is a rough draft or summary drawing, the same as a sketch of the main features.

clue.text: Figures of speech, for example, held back by single girl

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one, single

indicators.note: something held is gripped inside

parts.note: a girl's name

indicators.note: going back means running the other way

parts.note: e.g. means for example

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: examples of figurative language kept back by an unmarried young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'single girl' reads as unmarried, but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Imagery is the collective term for metaphors, similes and other figurative language in writing.
